{{< include ../exercise-header.qmd >}}


::: {#exr-leg-forget-pencil}
Suppose a model is used to predict the effect of an intervention in a real-world situation, for instance, a medical treatment. The model produces a logically correct result, but the model itself leaves out an important feature of the real situation. Which conclusion is most consistent with the chapter?

```{mcq}
#| label: d01-model-fault
1. The formal calculation can be correct even though the conclusion is not useful for the real-world situation. [correct]
2. The formal calculation must contain an arithmetic error.
3. The model must therefore be a fact rather than a representation.
4. Formal reasoning cannot be used with models.
```

:::
 <!-- end of exr-leg-forget-pencil -->
